title: Land, Water and Change
bigQuestion: Where is the water on Earth, and how do water and wind change the land?

story.title: Where Did the Rain Go?
story.kicker: A big rain fills the playground with puddles and little rivers. The next day they are gone. Where did all that water go?
paragraphs: It rained hard all morning. At recess, the playground was a new world. A puddle as big as a bus sat under the swings. Little rivers ran across the blacktop. They carried sand and leaves and one lost mitten.
Maya followed one little river. It ran downhill. It cut a tiny path through the sand pile. It joined another little river. Together they ran to a grate by the fence and disappeared.
Where the sand pile used to be flat, there was now a small ditch. The water had carried the sand away. It piled up in a fan near the grate. Maya poked it. 'The water moved the ground,' she said.
The next day the puddles were gone. The sand fan was still there. Water comes and goes. But the marks it leaves on the land can stay a long time.
story.think: Where do you think the water in the grate went? How could you find out?

lessons.title: Hills, Rivers, Lakes and Oceans
lessons.mainIdea: Earth has land, like hills and fields, and water, like rivers, lakes and oceans.
reading: Earth has two big kinds of places. Land and water. Land can be flat like a field. It can go up like a hill. Illinois is mostly flat, with some hills.
Water comes in many shapes. A *river* is water that flows along in a line. A *lake* is water with land all around it. An *ocean* is water so big you cannot see across it.
Chicago sits next to Lake Michigan. It is one of the biggest lakes in the world. You can stand on the beach and see no other side. But it is still a lake, not an ocean.

words.d: water that flows along in a line across the land
a body of water with land all around it
a very big body of salty water that covers most of Earth

look.title: From the Top of a Hill
look.text: Picture standing on a hill. Below you, a river winds like a ribbon. It flows into a wide blue lake. Fields spread out flat on both sides. Far away, a town sits by the water.
look.prompt: Name each kind of land and water you can see. Which is the river and which is the lake?

choices: Water with land all around it
check.why: A lake has land all the way around it.

check.q: Which is the biggest kind of water?
check.why: An ocean is so big you cannot see across it.

check.q: Is Lake Michigan a lake or an ocean?
check.why: It is huge, but it has land all around it. It is a lake.

lessons.title: Maps Show Where
lessons.mainIdea: A map is a drawing that shows where land and water are.
reading: A *map* is a drawing of a place from above. Like a bird would see it. On most maps, blue means water. Green or brown means land.
Find Illinois on a map of the United States. Look at the top right corner of the state. That blue is Lake Michigan. The wiggly line down the left side is the Mississippi River.
You can make a map too. Draw your playground from above. Show the hill. Show where the puddles form. Maps help people find their way and plan.

words.d: a drawing of a place as seen from above that shows where things are

look.title: A Map of the Playground
look.text: Here is a map drawn by a student. A big rectangle is the blacktop. A green circle is the grass. A small blue blob near the fence says 'puddle here after rain.' An arrow points downhill toward the grate.
look.prompt: What does the blue blob mean? Why did the student draw an arrow?

check.q: What color usually means water on a map?
check.why: On most maps, blue is water and green or brown is land.

check.q: A map shows a place from...
choices: above, like a bird sees it
check.why: A map is a drawing of a place seen from above.

check.q: The big blue shape at the top right of Illinois is...
check.why: Lake Michigan touches the top right corner of Illinois.

lessons.title: Most Water Is Salty
lessons.mainIdea: Most of Earth's water is in the salty ocean, and only a little is fresh.
reading: Look at a globe. Most of it is blue. The ocean covers most of Earth. Ocean water is *salty*. You cannot drink it. It would make you sick.
Only a small bit of Earth's water is *fresh*. Fresh water is not salty. Rivers, most lakes, rain and snow are fresh. That is the water we drink. Lake Michigan is fresh.
Out of every 100 cups of water on Earth, about 97 are salty ocean. Only about 3 are fresh. And most of those 3 are frozen in ice. So fresh water is precious. Do not waste it.

words.d: having salt in it, like ocean water
water that is not salty, like rain, rivers and most lakes

look.title: Earth's Water in 100 Cups
rows: Fresh water in rivers, lakes and underground
look.prompt: Which kind of water is there the most of? Which kind can we drink?

check.why: About 97 cups out of 100 are salty ocean water.
Ocean water is salty. Drinking it would make you sick.

check.q: Is Lake Michigan salty or fresh?
check.why: Lake Michigan is fresh water. Chicago drinks it.

lessons.title: Water and Ice
lessons.mainIdea: Water can be liquid or frozen ice, and cold turns one into the other.
reading: Water can be a *liquid*. It pours. It splashes. It fills a cup. When it gets very cold, water freezes. It turns to *ice*. Ice is hard. It keeps its shape.
In winter, ponds in Illinois freeze on top. Puddles turn to ice. Snow is tiny bits of ice. When spring comes, the ice melts back to water.
Freezing and melting go back and forth. Ice, water, ice, water. It is the same stuff. Only the cold changes it.

words.d: something that pours and takes the shape of its container, like water

look.title: The Ice Cube on the Table
look.text: Put an ice cube in a dish on the table. It is hard and cold. Come back after lunch. The dish holds a little puddle. Put the dish in the freezer. Come back tomorrow.
look.prompt: What will you find in the dish tomorrow? What made the ice change?

check.q: What happens to water when it gets very cold?
check.why: Very cold water freezes into hard ice.

check.q: What happens to ice in a warm room?
check.why: Warmth melts ice back into liquid water.

choices: the same stuff, cold or warm
check.why: Ice is frozen water. Melting turns it back. It is the same stuff.

lessons.title: Fast Change, Slow Change
lessons.mainIdea: Wind and water change the shape of the land, sometimes fast and sometimes slowly.
reading: Water can move the land. In our story, a little river cut a ditch in the sand pile. Real rivers do the same thing. They carry away dirt. That is *erosion*. Bit by bit, they carve their path.
Some changes are slow. A river bends a little more each year. It takes a lifetime to see. Some changes are fast. A *flood* can wash away a road in one day.
Wind moves land too. It blows sand into hills called dunes. The Indiana Dunes, near Chicago, were built by wind off Lake Michigan. That took thousands of years.

words.d: when wind or water carry away bits of land
when water rises and covers land that is usually dry

look.title: The Sand Pile Test
look.text: Make a small hill of sand in a tray. Pour a cup of water slowly on top. Watch what happens. Now make a new hill. Pour a whole pitcher of water on it fast.
look.prompt: Which pour changed the hill more? Which one is like a flood?

choices: Wind or water carrying away bits of land
check.why: Erosion is when wind or water carry land away, bit by bit.

check.q: Which is a fast change to the land?
choices: A river bending over many years
A flood washing out a road
A dune growing over thousands of years
check.why: A flood can change the land in one day. The others take years.
Wind off Lake Michigan blew sand into hills over thousands of years.

lessons.title: Slowing It Down
lessons.mainIdea: People can slow erosion by building walls and planting grass.
reading: Wind and water carry land away. People do not always like that. A house on a hill could slide. A beach could wash away. So people find ways to slow it down.
One way is a wall. A stone wall along a shore blocks big waves. Another way is plants. Grass and tree *roots* hold the dirt like fingers. Bare dirt washes away. Grassy dirt stays.
You can test it. Fill two trays with dirt. Put grass in one. Tilt them and pour water. Which tray loses more dirt?

words.d: the part of a plant that grows down into the dirt and holds it in place

look.title: Two Trays of Dirt
look.text: Two trays sit on a tilt. One holds bare dirt. The other holds dirt with grass growing in it. You pour the same cup of water on each. Muddy water runs out of one tray. Almost clear water runs out of the other.
look.prompt: Which tray gave muddy water? Why did the grass help?

check.q: How do grass roots help the land?
choices: They hold the dirt in place
check.why: Roots grip the dirt like fingers, so water cannot carry it off.

check.q: What could people build to block big waves?
check.why: A stone wall along a shore blocks waves and slows erosion.
Bare dirt has no roots to hold it, so it washes away.

review.q: Which is water flowing in a line?
review.why: A river flows along in a line across the land.
About 97 cups out of 100 are salty ocean water.
A map is a drawing from above that shows where things are.

review.q: What happens to a puddle when it gets very cold?
review.why: Very cold water freezes into ice.

review.q: Which is a slow change to the land?
choices: A river bend growing over many years
review.why: A river bend grows a little each year. That is slow.

review.q: Why do people plant grass on a bare hill?
choices: To hold the dirt and slow erosion
review.why: Roots hold the dirt so wind and water cannot carry it away.
